title: Play: The Glue That Connects Us
author: John McLean
summary: John McLean, writing as Wisdom From Dad, argues that fathers who work hard to provide often forget that play is what binds a family together. He tells the story of two weeks every summer on Balboa Island, noting that the last family vacation felt different because the play had stopped. He then recounts twenty years of weekends at Lake Havasu with friends and their children, and a leadership retreat where twelve grown men built sandcastles and found their creativity and friendships improved. His weekly tenet is to play gleefully, supported by Stuart Brown's book on play and Aristotle's view that a good life requires enjoying worthwhile activities. The practice he assigns is concrete: put the phone away and do something simply because it is enjoyable, from Lego to shooting hoops to cards. He closes by reminding dads that children will remember how it felt to be with them.
points: McLean treats play as a bond-building practice rather than a reward earned after work, since for an ambitious man the work is never finished.
Looking back, he can see how easily a family drifts apart when it stops making time to play together.
He extends the principle to business, describing how a sandcastle-building afternoon with fellow regional directors fuelled creativity and solidified friendships more than golf or dinners had.
The weekly practice is to put down the phone and invite wife and children into an activity chosen purely for enjoyment, without turning it into a teaching opportunity.
He reminds fathers that their responsibility includes showing children how to enjoy the present, not only providing for and preparing them for the future.
quotes: We still had a nice vacation that summer, but something had changed; the play had stopped. Now, almost fifty years later, I can see how easily we can begin to drift apart when we stop making time to play together.
When you work, work with focus, diligence and grit, but taking time to play not only recharges the battery, it connects team members and fosters creativity.
Play isn’t just a reward we earn after the work is finished, because let’s face it – if you’re ambitious, the work is never finished.
So, this week, I encourage you to make room for a little more fun. Put down the phone, close the laptop, and invite your wife and kids to do something simply because it’s enjoyable.
Over 2,300 years ago, Aristotle recognized that a good life requires more than hard work, and that living well requires learning how to enjoy worthwhile activities, not simply how to be productive.

But all work and no play is a strategy that most often backfires, because good family memories aren’t made when you’re out there achieving your goals. They’re made when we put the work aside and simply enjoy being together.

Not every moment needs to be turned into a teaching opportunity and you certainly don’t need to make everything productive. Sometimes, the best thing you can do for your family is simply enjoy being together.
Your kids won’t remember everything you did for them, but they’ll remember how it felt to be with you.
